prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Multifrequency VLBA observations of the final group of ten objects in a sample of FIRST-based compact steep spectrum (CSS) sources are presented. The sample was selected to investigate whether objects of this kind could be relics of radio-loud AGNs switched off at very early stages of their evolution or possibly to indicate intermittent activity. Initial observations were made using MERLIN at 5 GHz. The sources have now been observed with the VLBA at 1.7, 5 and 8.4 GHz in a snapshot mode with phase-referencing. The resulting maps are presented along with unpublished 8.4-GHz VLA images of five sources. Some of the sources discussed here show a complex radio morphology and therefore a complicated past that, in some cases, might indicate intermittent activity. One of the sources studied - 1045+352 - is known as a powerful radio and infrared-luminous broad absorption line (BAL) quasar. It is a young CSS object whose asymmetric two-sided morphology on a scale of several hundred parsecs, extending in two different directions, may suggest intermittent activity. The young age and compact structure of 1045+352 is consistent with the evolution scenario of BAL quasars. It has also been confirmed that the submillimetre flux of 1045+352 can be seriously contaminated by synchrotron emission.

We present multifrequency VLBA observations of the final ten objects in a sample of FIRST-based compact steep-spectrum (CSS) sources. The sample was selected to investigate whether such objects could be relics of radio-loud AGNs that switched off at very early stages of their evolution or might instead indicate intermittent activity. Initial observations were conducted with MERLIN at 5 GHz. The sources have now been observed with the VLBA at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz in phase-referenced snapshot mode. The resulting maps are presented alongside unpublished 8.4-GHz VLA images of five sources.

Several of the sources discussed here exhibit complex radio morphologies and, consequently, complicated evolutionary histories that may, in some cases, indicate intermittent activity. One of the sources studied, 1045+352, is known to be a powerful radio and infrared-luminous broad absorption line (BAL) quasar. It is a young CSS object with an asymmetric, two-sided morphology extending in two different directions on scales of several hundred parsecs, possibly suggesting intermittent activity. The young age and compact structure of 1045+352 are consistent with the evolutionary scenario for BAL quasars. It has also been confirmed that the submillimetre flux of 1045+352 may be significantly contaminated by synchrotron emission.
outputs.L2:
We present multifrequency VLBA observations of the last ten sources in a FIRST-selected sample of compact steep-spectrum (CSS) objects. This sample was assembled to determine whether such sources might represent radio-loud AGNs that ceased operating during the earliest phases of their development or, alternatively, exhibit episodic activity. The objects were first observed with MERLIN at 5 GHz and have since been imaged with the VLBA at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz using phase-referenced snapshot observations. The resulting maps are shown together with previously unpublished VLA images at 8.4 GHz for five of the sources.

Several objects display intricate radio structures, implying complex evolutionary histories that may, in certain cases, point to intermittent activity. Among them, 1045+352 is a known powerful broad absorption line (BAL) quasar with strong radio and infrared emission. This young CSS source has an asymmetric, two-sided morphology spanning several hundred parsecs and extending along two distinct directions, a configuration that may be evidence of episodic activity. Its compact structure and youth agree with the proposed evolutionary framework for BAL quasars. The observations also confirm that synchrotron radiation can substantially contaminate the measured submillimetre flux of 1045+352.
outputs.L3:
Multifrequency Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) observations were conducted for the final ten objects in a FIRST-based sample of compact steep-spectrum (CSS) radio sources. The primary aim was to determine whether these compact sources are relics of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs) that ceased activity at an early stage of their evolution or, alternatively, systems undergoing recurrent or intermittent episodes of activity.

The sources were observed at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz, with complementary imaging from MERLIN and the Very Large Array (VLA). These combined data revealed complex radio morphologies in several objects, providing evidence that their evolutionary histories may be more complicated than a single, continuous phase of jet activity.

Particular attention was given to the broad absorption line (BAL) quasar 1045+352. Its compact steep-spectrum characteristics indicate that it is a young radio source, while its asymmetric structure, extending in two distinct directions, may reflect changes in jet orientation or separate episodes of nuclear activity. This interpretation supports models in which BAL quasars represent an early evolutionary phase marked by episodic or restarting AGN activity.

The study also found that the measured submillimetre flux of 1045+352 may not arise solely from thermal dust emission. A potentially substantial contribution from synchrotron radiation could contaminate the submillimetre measurements, and this effect should be considered when estimating the source’s dust content and star-formation properties.
outputs.L4:
Compact steep-spectrum (CSS) radio sources are generally interpreted as young active galactic nuclei whose radio jets are still confined to the central regions of their host galaxies. Their small sizes and often distorted structures, however, may also reflect interactions with a dense interstellar medium or repeated cycles of nuclear activity. To investigate these possibilities, ten CSS sources were observed with the Very Long Baseline Array at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz. The milliarcsecond-resolution data were supplemented with MERLIN and Very Large Array images, providing sensitivity to radio structures over a wider range of angular scales.

The multifrequency observations made it possible to compare source morphologies and construct radio spectra for individual components. This helped distinguish likely flat-spectrum cores from steep-spectrum jets and lobes, while also revealing diffuse or disconnected features that could represent remnants of earlier activity. Although not every source displayed an unambiguous radio core, several had complex, asymmetric, or misaligned structures inconsistent with a single, simple episode of jet production. Such morphologies can arise when an AGN switches off and later restarts, potentially with a changed jet direction, although strong interactions between the jets and the surrounding gas may produce similar effects.

The most notable object in the sample is the young broad-absorption-line quasar 1045+352. Its compact radio emission is strongly asymmetric and contains components oriented along different position angles, indicating a complicated history of jet propagation. The structure can be interpreted as evidence for more than one phase of activity, with newer ejecta following a direction different from that of older radio plasma. Alternatively, deflection by a dense and inhomogeneous interstellar medium may have contributed to the observed bending. In either case, the source appears to be a young system in which the radio jets are still interacting strongly with the central environment.

These properties are consistent with evolutionary models in which broad-absorption-line quasars represent an early stage of quasar development. In this picture, the active nucleus is initially surrounded by substantial amounts of gas and dust. Powerful outflows and newly formed radio jets then begin to clear this material, producing the broad blueshifted absorption features characteristic of BAL quasars. The distorted and asymmetric radio morphology of 1045+352 supports the idea that the source is being observed during this transitional phase rather than being explained solely by orientation effects.

The broadband spectrum of 1045+352 also has implications for estimates of its dust emission and star-formation activity. Extrapolation of the radio synchrotron spectrum to submillimetre wavelengths shows that a significant fraction of the measured submillimetre flux can be produced by the radio source itself. The submillimetre emission therefore cannot be attributed entirely to thermal radiation from dust. Any estimate of the dust mass, infrared luminosity, or star-formation rate must first account for this synchrotron contribution.

Overall, the observations demonstrate that high-resolution, multifrequency radio imaging is essential for identifying possible shutdown and restarting phases in compact AGN. Several members of the sample show structures compatible with intermittent activity, although environmental interactions remain an important alternative explanation. The results for 1045+352 are particularly suggestive: its complex radio morphology, youth, BAL characteristics, and synchrotron-contaminated submillimetre emission together portray an AGN undergoing rapid evolution within a dense and disturbed nuclear environment.
outputs.L5:
### Multifrequency VLBA Studies with FIRST

Multifrequency observations with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) provide a powerful method for investigating the compact radio structures of active galactic nuclei and other extragalactic sources. Targets selected from the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty Centimeters (FIRST) survey can be studied at several VLBA frequencies to determine their morphology, spectral properties, and brightness temperatures on milliarcsecond scales.

By comparing images obtained at different frequencies, astronomers can distinguish flat-spectrum radio cores from steep-spectrum jets and lobes. Multifrequency VLBA data also reveal synchrotron self-absorption, spectral aging, and frequency-dependent shifts in the apparent position of the radio core. Combining the wide-area coverage of FIRST with the high angular resolution of the VLBA therefore offers an effective approach to identifying young radio sources, compact jets, and obscured active galactic nuclei.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a radio astronomy paper presenting multifrequency VLBA observations of the final ten FIRST-selected compact steep spectrum sources, including the findings for BAL quasar 1045+352.
counterfactuals.output: We present multifrequency Very Long Baseline Array observations of the final ten compact steep-spectrum sources selected from the VLA FIRST survey. The milliarcsecond-resolution images, together with spectral-index information and earlier arcsecond-scale data, reveal a heterogeneous population of compact doubles, core–jet systems, and complex or distorted sources. Several objects show pronounced asymmetries, jet bending, and resolved-out low-surface-brightness emission, indicating strong interactions with the surrounding interstellar medium and, in some cases, possible recurrent activity. Particular attention is given to the radio-loud broad-absorption-line quasar 1045+352. Its frequency-dependent structure identifies the compact core and shows a sharply changing jet direction on parsec scales. The complex morphology is consistent with a young or restarted jet whose propagation has been affected by precession and/or interaction with dense gas associated with the BAL outflow. These observations complete the VLBA imaging of the FIRST-selected sample and support the view that compact steep-spectrum sources are predominantly young radio objects, while demonstrating that their early evolution can be strongly modified by nuclear activity and the gaseous environment of the host galaxy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study of ten CSS radio sources observed with MERLIN, the VLBA, and the VLA, focusing on evidence for relic or intermittent AGN activity.
counterfactuals.output:
The study used complementary resolutions to examine ten compact steep-spectrum (CSS) radio sources: the VLBA traced parsec-scale cores and jets, MERLIN mapped their sub-kiloparsec structure, and the VLA searched for faint emission on larger scales.

The main evidence for relic or intermittent AGN activity was:

- **Diffuse, low-surface-brightness emission outside the compact CSS structures**, interpreted as remnants of an earlier jet episode.
- **Misalignments between inner VLBA jets and outer MERLIN/VLA features**, suggesting that the source restarted with a changed jet direction.
- **Compact “fader” candidates** with steep spectra but no obvious flat-spectrum core, hotspots, or well-collimated jets, consistent with activity having recently ceased.
- In some objects, **a currently active compact core embedded within older emission**, giving a particularly strong restarted-source interpretation.

Not every irregular feature required recurrent activity: jet interaction with a dense, asymmetric interstellar medium could also produce distorted or one-sided morphologies. Nevertheless, the combined observations indicated that CSS sources are not uniformly young objects evolving continuously into large radio galaxies. Some undergo short-lived or repeated outbursts, leaving relic plasma around a newly active—or already fading—compact source.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise scientific abstract describing 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz VLBA snapshot observations of compact steep spectrum sources and their complex radio morphologies.
counterfactuals.output: We present multi-frequency Very Long Baseline Array snapshot observations of compact steep-spectrum (CSS) radio sources at 1.7, 5.0, and 8.4 GHz. The milliarcsecond-resolution images reveal diverse and complex morphologies, including asymmetric doubles, core–jet structures, compact symmetric objects, bent jets, and diffuse low-surface-brightness emission. Comparison across frequencies enables component spectral indices to be determined and candidate flat-spectrum cores to be distinguished from steep-spectrum jets, lobes, and hotspots. The pronounced asymmetries and distortions observed in several sources suggest interactions between young radio outflows and an inhomogeneous circumnuclear medium, although relativistic beaming may contribute in some cases. These results demonstrate that nominally compact CSS sources frequently contain intricate parsec-scale structures and support a scenario in which many are young radio galaxies evolving through dense host-galaxy environments.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the observational results for the final group of objects in a FIRST-based CSS sample, with particular attention to the morphology, evolutionary status, and submillimetre contamination of 1045+352.
counterfactuals.output:
The last set of sources observed from the FIRST-selected compact steep-spectrum (CSS) sample did not form a morphologically uniform population. Higher-resolution MERLIN/VLBI imaging divided them among unresolved or barely resolved objects, compact doubles, and asymmetric core–jet or triple systems. Weak cores, unequal lobes, bends, and diffuse low-surface-brightness extensions were common. Thus, although most are genuinely compact and probably young radio sources, some show evidence that CSS evolution is intermittent: jets can be disrupted by a dense interstellar medium, switch off, restart, or change direction rather than simply grow into classical large FR II galaxies.

### 1045+352

1045+352, a radio-loud broad-absorption-line quasar, is the most striking example.

- **Morphology:** Its radio emission is strongly bent and consists of components lying along different position angles. The innermost structure is interpreted as a comparatively recent jet, whereas more extended emission traces an earlier direction of activity. A simple, symmetric young double does not explain the observations well.
- **Evolutionary interpretation:** It is still a young CSS quasar, but probably one experiencing renewed or redirected activity. Jet precession, a merger-induced change of the central-engine axis, and interaction with a dense circumnuclear medium can all contribute. The source therefore supports an evolutionary picture in which the BAL phenomenon and CSS phase occur while the quasar is still clearing gas and dust from its surroundings, possibly during a restarted episode.
- **Submillimetre emission:** The reported SCUBA 850-µm detection cannot safely be treated as pure thermal dust emission. Extrapolation of the compact radio synchrotron spectrum indicates that a substantial—and, depending on the assumed high-frequency spectral break, potentially dominant—part of the 850-µm flux can be synchrotron radiation. Consequently, dust mass, far-infrared luminosity, and star-formation rate inferred by assigning the entire submillimetre flux to cold dust would be overestimated.

In short, 1045+352 is best regarded as a young, disturbed and probably recurrent/reoriented radio source, while its apparent submillimetre brightness provides only an upper limit on the thermal dust contribution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a journal-style astronomy abstract about whether young compact radio sources can be remnants of prematurely switched-off AGNs, mentioning phase-referenced VLBA imaging and the BAL quasar 1045+352.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We investigate whether a fraction of young, compact radio sources represent short-lived active galactic nuclei (AGNs) whose jets were switched off before developing large-scale radio structures. Phase-referenced Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) imaging is used to trace weak, low-surface-brightness emission and to distinguish active compact jets from fading lobes on parsec scales. The resulting morphologies show that some compact steep-spectrum objects lack the prominent terminal hotspots expected in continuously powered young sources, consistent instead with rapidly fading remnants or recurrent nuclear activity. The broad-absorption-line (BAL) quasar 1045+352 provides a particularly instructive case: its complex, misaligned radio components suggest multiple episodes of jet production and changes in propagation direction, plausibly caused by intermittency and interaction with a dense circumnuclear medium. Although compactness alone cannot establish a remnant origin, the VLBA observations support a scenario in which at least some young radio sources undergo premature jet cessation and never evolve into extended radio galaxies. Such short duty cycles may be common during early, gas-rich phases of AGN and quasar evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
